description: Hi, I’m Hrishi, a first-year Aerospace Engineering student at Nottingham (Python, C++). We’re building Polar Window: an interactive tool comparing lunar south pole landing sites and dates by Sun and Earth visibility, using real JPL Horizons data, with a best-start-date scanner and a plain-English mode. Looking for help with LOLA terrain horizons, a planetary science or mission-ops sanity check, and design/comms for the pitch. Any experience level welcome. Message me!
summary:
Polar Window is a single-page web tool for comparing lunar south pole landing sites and dates in seconds. It combines hourly JPL Horizons (DE441) Sun and Earth positions, including libration, with real LOLA terrain horizons for eight south polar sites, so users see when the Sun and Earth actually clear the local skyline, not just a flat horizon.

Users compare two sites side by side with a sky dome, a skyline panorama and a timeline, with countdowns to sunset and Earthset. A heatmap shows every site against every start date, so a planner facing a launch slip can find an alternative immediately. A best-start-date finder, plain-English mode and a one-minute tour serve planners, educators and the public.

Terrain changes the answer. Over 8 Oct 2026 to 1 Mar 2027, Malapert has Sun and Earth both up 82% of the time with terrain, versus 48% on a flat horizon, while Haworth drops from 41% to 8%. A flat-horizon tool would rank these sites differently, which is why accessible, terrain-aware planning matters for mission power and communications.
details:
Polar Window is a web tool for comparing lunar south pole landing sites and start dates in seconds. Users pick two sites and a date and see how the Sun and Earth move against the real local skyline, shown three ways: a sky dome, an azimuth-by-elevation skyline panorama, and a timeline. It shows countdowns to sunset and Earthset, the share of time Sun and Earth are both up, and the longest stretch of darkness. A heatmap compares all sites across every possible start date, so a planner facing a launch slip can find an alternative immediately. A best-start-date finder, an auto-written verdict, a plain-English mode and a one-minute tour serve non-specialists.

Under the hood:

Sun and Earth positions are hourly JPL Horizons (DE441) data covering 8 Oct 2026 to 1 Mar 2027, including libration and without refraction. We computed them once at the original site coordinates and rotated them exactly to each final site, including Earth’s parallax. We checked this against Horizons data at other sites and it matched to within about 0.02° in elevation.

Terrain horizons come from the 80 m LOLA polar elevation model. From each site we cast rays every 1° of azimuth out to 100 km, including lunar curvature, to build a skyline profile. A body counts as “up” only when it clears the skyline in its own direction.

What are the benefits?

Planners get an answer in seconds instead of moving between several expert tools. Terrain changes the answer: over the data window, Malapert has Sun and Earth both up 82% of the time with real terrain, against 48% on a flat horizon, while Haworth drops from 41% to 8%. The tool also stays usable for educators and the public.

What is the intended impact?

We want to shorten early site and date screening, help teams react quickly when schedules slip, and show students and the public why the lunar south pole is such a hard place to land.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (vanilla JS and canvas) for the app, as a single self-contained page.

Python (numpy, rasterio, matplotlib) for the terrain processing, run on a personal laptop. No special hardware.

Data: JPL Horizons; the LOLA south polar elevation model (LDEM_80S_80MPP_ADJ, NASA PGDA); LROC candidate-region coordinates; and published landing-region coordinates from ESA and journal papers.

AI: Claude was used for helping within the fields of coding, analysis, debugging and building.

How is it creative?

It puts the difference between a flat horizon and real terrain on screen, which reorders the site rankings.

It turns the question “the launch slipped, now what?” into a single clickable heatmap.

It rotates one validated Horizons dataset to any site, instead of querying every location separately.

It shows the skyline in two forms: as a dome from above and as a panorama.

What factors did we consider?

Accuracy: libration, Earth parallax, curvature, no atmospheric refraction, and a check that the DEM projection matches our coordinate conversion.

Honest limits: results cover a 5-month window, not annual illumination. Each site is a crest point, a best case, not a landing ellipse. The 80 m model slightly smooths narrow ridges. Sun up is not the same as power, and Earth in view is not the same as a comms link. Sites without terrain data are clearly hatched.

Audiences: one interface for planners, educators and the public.

Provenance: where every coordinate and dataset came from.
